Hermitage. The largest art museum in Russia, the Hermitage is housed in the Winter Palace and adjacent buildings in Saint Petersburg, making it one of the world's oldest museums, founded by Catherine the Great in 1764. The Winter Palace complex itself is a baroque architectural masterpiece. Catherine built this as her private collection, and the adjacent galleries evolved as she continued acquiring art over decades. The museum contains over three million artworks, including masterpieces by Rembrandt, Caravaggio, Titian, Rubens, and Matisse—a testament to royal acquisition over two centuries. The collection is particularly strong in Dutch and Flemish paintings, Impressionist and Post-Impressionist works, and Russian imperial acquisitions from across Europe and the Mediterranean. The building's layout evolved organically as wings were added over time, and visitors navigate through opulent rooms that were themselves designed as galleries. The museum's character transformed after the October Revolution in 1917, when the Bolsheviks turned it into a monument to revolutionary people's culture. Within the complex stands the Hermitage Theatre, an eighteenth-century structure that is distinct in itself, and the basement holds an archaeology museum that preserves finds from Russian imperial excavations. Catherine's acquisitive patronage not only founded this extraordinary collection but established Russian imperial taste for generations to come. The Hermitage remains inseparable from Saint Petersburg's identity as a cultural capital and reflects the Romanov aesthetic through centuries of international diplomacy in art.
